newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean union seeks double-digit wage hike.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean union seeks double-digit wage hike.

text.p: South Korea's government-sanctioned labour union said on Friday it would seek an average 11.2 percent wage increase for this year and refrain from strike action for at least a month.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions, South Korea's largest umbrella labour union, largely stayed away from recent labour strife sparked by a controversial labour law.
The federation said it would encourage political parties to revise the law and would seek an additional 7.2 percent wage increase if the revised version did not conform with international standards.

After nearly a month of wildcat strikes organised by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, President Kim Young-sam made a dramatic concession last week to send the law back to parliament.

The law, which makes it easier for companies to sack workers and replace strikers, was rammed through parliament by the ruling New Korea Party on December 26 in a dawn session while opposition deputies slept.

"Until the end of February, we will refrain from strikes...to encourage political negotiations for the revision of the labour law. Instead we will focus on production," federation president Park In-sang told reporters.
He said the proposed 11.2 percent increase took into account the rise in the cost of living. Consumer prices rose by an estimated 4.5 percent in 1996.
Wage negotiations normally begin in late February in South Korea although any agreement would be retroactive to January 1.
Government officials said South Korean companies should stop allowing double-digit wage hikes which hamper their international competitiveness.
Park said the federation planned to organise an all-out one-day strike on May 1, Labour Day, unless there was a satisfactory revision of the labour law.
A two-day strike call by the group earlier this month fizzled out due to poor response.
